tool.name: OpenCV
tool.tagline: The standard library for computer vision and image processing
tool.description: OpenCV is a large C++ computer vision library with first-class Python bindings (cv2) that work directly on NumPy arrays. It covers image I/O, filtering, geometry, feature detection, video, camera calibration and running neural networks. It is the default toolbox for preprocessing images, classic vision pipelines and real-time video work.

glossary.def: A large open-source library for working with images and video: loading and saving them, filtering, finding shapes, tracking motion and more. Its Python package is imported as cv2.
One tiny square of colour in a digital image. An image is a grid of pixels, each storing a few numbers for its colour or brightness.
One of the numbers stored per pixel, such as the amount of blue, green or red. A colour image usually has 3 channels; a grayscale image has 1.
An image with only brightness and no colour: one number per pixel, from 0 (black) to 255 (white).
OpenCV's channel order for colour images: blue, green, red. Most other software uses RGB, so the first and last channels must be swapped when passing images between them.
In OpenCV arithmetic, to stop at the smallest or largest allowed value instead of wrapping around: for uint8, 250 + 10 gives 255, not 4.
An extra channel in some images that says how see-through each pixel is, from fully transparent to fully solid.
Without a screen or window system. A headless OpenCV package works on servers but cannot open windows with imshow.
A way of describing colours with numbers, such as BGR (amounts of blue, green, red light) or HSV (hue, saturation, brightness).
A colour space that stores hue (which colour), saturation (how strong) and value (how bright) separately, so a colour can be picked out despite changing light.
A colour space with one lightness channel and two colour channels, arranged so equal number differences look like roughly equal colour differences to people.
Drawing edges with in-between shades on the border pixels so that lines and text look smooth instead of jagged.
An image's width divided by its height. Keeping it the same when resizing stops the picture from looking stretched or squashed.
Estimating the values of new pixels from the surrounding old ones, as needed when an image is resized, rotated or warped.
Fitting an image into a fixed size without stretching it: shrink it to fit, then fill the leftover strips with a plain colour, like the bars around a widescreen film.
Turning an image into black and white by comparing every pixel with a chosen value (the threshold): brighter pixels become white, the rest black.
In OpenCV, a single-channel uint8 image where selected pixels are 255 (white) and all others 0 (black), used to mark which pixels belong to something.
A way to pick a threshold automatically: it chooses the brightness value that best separates the image's dark and bright groups of pixels.
In images, random speckles of wrong brightness or colour, mostly caused by the camera sensor, especially in low light.
In image processing, a small grid of numbers slid over the image; each output pixel is computed from the pixels under it. (Not the operating-system kernel.)
Noise made of isolated pure white and pure black pixels scattered over an image.
Sliding a kernel over an image and, at each position, multiplying the pixels under it by the kernel's weights and adding them up to give one output pixel.
Operations that grow, shrink or tidy the white shapes in a binary mask by sliding a small shape (the structuring element) over it.
The small shape, such as a 3x3 square or a disc, that morphology slides over a mask to decide how shapes grow or shrink.
A morphology step that shrinks white shapes: a pixel stays white only if the whole structuring element fits inside white.
A morphology step that grows white shapes: a pixel becomes white if the structuring element touches any white pixel.
In an image, a place where brightness changes sharply, such as the border between an object and its background.
In an image, how fast and in which direction brightness changes from one pixel to the next. Large gradients mark edges.
A classic method for finding edges that produces thin, connected edge lines, using two thresholds to decide which pixels are edges.
Keeping only the strongest of several overlapping responses and dropping the rest: the strongest pixel across an edge, or the best box among overlapping detections.
Using two thresholds: values above the high one are accepted, values between the two only if they connect to an accepted one. It keeps edges continuous without letting in noise.
Remapping brightness values so they are spread evenly over the whole range, which increases contrast in dull images.
Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalisation: improving contrast tile by tile across an image while capping how far it is boosted, so noise isn't exaggerated.
The outline of one region in a binary mask, stored as the list of points along its edge.
The centre point of a shape: the average position of all its pixels.
The outline of a shape with every dent filled in, like a rubber band stretched around it.
One still image in a video. A video is a sequence of frames shown quickly one after another.
How many frames a video shows per second, often 25 or 30.
The method used to compress video frames into a file and unpack them again, such as MJPG or H.264; OpenCV picks one by a four-character code (fourcc).
Detecting moving things in video by learning what the empty scene looks like and marking pixels that differ from it.
An estimate of how each point or pixel moves from one video frame to the next.
A change of an image's geometry that combines rotating, scaling, shifting and slanting; straight lines stay straight. Stored as a 2x3 matrix.
In geometry, shifting every point by the same amount in x and y without rotating or resizing.
Slanting an image, like pushing the top of a deck of cards sideways while the bottom stays put.
A change of geometry that can map any four-sided shape onto any other, such as turning a tilted photo of a page into a flat, straight-on view.
The 3x3 matrix describing a perspective transform between two views of a flat surface.
A distinctive spot in an image, such as a corner, that can be found again in another photo of the same scene.
A list of numbers summarising the small patch of image around a keypoint, used to find the same spot in another image.
The number of positions at which two strings of bits differ; used to compare binary descriptors.
A method that finds a model, such as a homography, despite wrong data: it repeatedly fits the model to a few random matches and keeps the one most matches agree with.
A data point or match that agrees with the fitted model, as opposed to an outlier.
A camera's 3x3 matrix holding how strongly its lens magnifies (focal length, in pixels) and where the lens centre falls on the image.
A few numbers describing how a camera lens bends straight lines, so the distortion can be removed from images.
How far, in pixels, the points a fitted camera model predicts are from the points actually detected. Small values mean a good calibration.
The position and orientation of an object (or camera) in 3-D space.
A common file format for trained neural networks, so a network trained in one library (such as PyTorch) can be run in another (such as OpenCV).
In cv2.dnn, the 4-D float32 array a neural network takes as input, in NCHW layout. (Elsewhere, 'blob' also means a solid patch in a mask.)
The order of axes in a neural network's input: number of images, channels, height, width.
Glue code that lets Python call a library written in another language, here C++, converting arguments and results between the two.
OpenCV's C++ image type: a small description of the rows, columns and element type plus a pointer to the pixel data.
A standard way to run calculations on graphics chips and other accelerators; OpenCV can use it through UMat.
A precomputed list of answers, one for every possible input (for uint8, 256 values), so each pixel is converted by a quick look-up instead of a calculation.
OpenCV's extra modules, contributed by the community and less settled than the main ones, shipped in the opencv-contrib-python packages.

concepts.name: Images are NumPy arrays
concepts.summary: In cv2 an image is just a NumPy array: height x width x channels, usually uint8, with the colours in BGR order.
concepts.why: Every OpenCV call takes and returns NumPy arrays, so knowing the layout lets you mix cv2 with plain NumPy freely.
concepts.body:
A digital photo is a grid of tiny coloured squares called **pixels**. A 640 x 480 photo is 640 pixels across and 480 down. Each pixel stores a few numbers saying how much of each basic colour it contains; each of those numbers is a **channel**.

**OpenCV** is a large library for working with images and video. It is written in C++, a fast compiled language, and from Python you import it as `cv2`. In Python an image is simply a NumPy array: there is no special image type to learn.

The layout is fixed by convention:

- A colour image has shape `(height, width, 3)`: rows first, then columns, then the 3 channels.
- A **grayscale** (black-and-white) image has shape `(height, width)`: one brightness number per pixel and no channel axis.
- The usual dtype is `uint8`, values 0 (none) to 255 (full). Some operations give `float32` or `int16` results instead, when values can have fractions or go negative.

OpenCV stores the three channels in **BGR** order (blue, green, red), not the RGB order (red, green, blue) most other software uses. It is a historical choice that trips up every newcomer: pixel `img[y, x]` gives `[blue, green, red]`.

Because indexing is `img[row, col]`, the **y coordinate comes first** when you index. But OpenCV functions that take points, sizes or rectangles use `(x, y)` and `(width, height)`. Keep both conventions in mind: NumPy indexing is `(y, x)`, cv2 arguments are `(x, y)`.

Since an image is an array, you can create one with `np.zeros`, crop it with slicing and change its brightness with arithmetic. Watch the dtype, though: NumPy `uint8` arithmetic wraps around (250 + 10 gives 4), while `cv2.add` **saturates**: it stops at the limit, so 250 + 10 gives 255.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.zeros((120, 200, 3), dtype=np.uint8)   # black, 200 wide x 120 tall
img[:, :100] = (255, 0, 0)                      # left half BLUE (BGR!)
print(img.shape, img.dtype)                     # (120, 200, 3) uint8
print(img[10, 10])                              # [255   0   0]

h, w = img.shape[:2]
print("width", w, "height", h)                  # width 200 height 120

a = np.array([[250]], dtype=np.uint8)
print(a + np.uint8(10))                         # [[4]]   NumPy wraps
print(cv2.add(a, np.array([[10]], np.uint8)))  # [[255]] OpenCV saturates
takeaways: An image is an ndarray of shape (h, w) or (h, w, channels), usually uint8
Colour channels are BGR, not RGB
Index as img[y, x]; cv2 functions take points as (x, y)
cv2 arithmetic saturates, NumPy uint8 arithmetic wraps
pitfalls: Passing `img.shape[:2]` (h, w) where cv2 expects a size `(w, h)`, which swaps width and height.

quiz.q: A colour image has shape (480, 640, 3). What is its width in pixels?
quiz.explain: Shape is (height, width, channels), so width is the second number.

quiz.q: `img[5, 2]` on a BGR image returns `[0, 0, 255]`. What colour is that pixel?
quiz.explain: The last channel in BGR order is red, so only red is at full intensity.

concepts.name: Reading, writing and showing images
concepts.summary: Load images with cv2.imread, save them with cv2.imwrite and show them in a window with imshow plus waitKey.
concepts.why: Getting pixels in and out reliably is the first step of every image script, and imread fails without raising an error.
concepts.body:
`cv2.imread(path, flags)` loads an image file, such as a JPEG or PNG photo, into a NumPy array. The flag picks what you get:

- `cv2.IMREAD_COLOR` (default): 3 channels in BGR order; any transparency is dropped
- `cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE`: a single brightness channel
- `cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED`: the file exactly as stored, including an **alpha channel** (a fourth channel saying how see-through each pixel is) and the 16-bit values, 0 to 65535, that some PNG files use

The big gotcha: **imread does not raise an exception** for a missing or unreadable file. It returns `None`, and the error only shows up later as a confusing `'NoneType' object has no attribute 'shape'`. Always check the result.

`cv2.imwrite(path, img, params)` picks the format from the **file extension** (the `.png` or `.jpg` at the end of the name) and returns `True` on success. Optional params control how hard the file is **compressed** (packed into fewer bytes), for example `[cv2.IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY, 90]` or `[cv2.IMWRITE_PNG_COMPRESSION, 9]`.

Sometimes an image never touches a file: it arrives as bytes over the internet or is kept in a **database** (an organised store of data). `cv2.imencode('.png', img)` turns an array into the bytes of a PNG file and returns `(ok, buffer)`; `cv2.imdecode(np_bytes, flags)` does the reverse. This is also the workaround for file paths with non-English characters on Windows, which `imread` cannot open.

For a quick look, `cv2.imshow(window_name, img)` opens a window on screen, but nothing appears until you call `cv2.waitKey(ms)`, which gives the window time to draw itself and to notice key presses; `waitKey(0)` waits until a key is pressed. Finish with `cv2.destroyAllWindows()`.

Windows need a screen. On a **server** (a computer in a data centre that you control remotely, with no screen) there is nowhere to show them, and the `opencv-python-headless` package leaves window support out entirely; **headless** means 'without a display'.

In a Jupyter **notebook** (a page in your browser where you run Python in small cells) `imshow` doesn't work well either. There, convert the image to RGB and show it with matplotlib, Python's common plotting library.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.full((60, 80, 3), (0, 128, 255), np.uint8)    # orange in BGR
ok = cv2.imwrite("orange.png", img)
print(ok)                                         # True

back = cv2.imread("orange.png")                   # BGR uint8
print(back.shape, back[0, 0])                     # (60, 80, 3) [  0 128 255]
gray = cv2.imread("orange.png", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
print(gray.shape)                                 # (60, 80)

missing = cv2.imread("no_such_file.jpg")
print(missing is None)                            # True -- no exception!

ok, buf = cv2.imencode(".jpg", img, [cv2.IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY, 90])
print(ok, buf.dtype)                              # True uint8 (encoded bytes)
decoded = cv2.imdecode(buf, cv2.IMREAD_COLOR)
print(decoded.shape)                              # (60, 80, 3)
takeaways: `imread` returns None instead of raising: always check it
The flag chooses colour, grayscale or unchanged (alpha, 16-bit)
`imwrite` picks the format from the extension; `imencode`/`imdecode` work in memory
`imshow` needs `waitKey` to actually draw
pitfalls: Calling `cv2.imshow` without `cv2.waitKey`, so the window never paints, or using it on a headless install.

quiz.q: What does `cv2.imread('typo.jpg')` do if the file does not exist?
quiz.explain: imread signals failure by returning None, so you must check the result yourself.

quiz.q: You need to keep a PNG's transparency when loading it. Which flag do you use?
quiz.explain: IMREAD_UNCHANGED keeps the alpha channel and original bit depth.

concepts.name: Colour spaces and cvtColor
concepts.summary: Convert between BGR, RGB, grayscale and HSV with cv2.cvtColor, and know why HSV is used for picking colours.
concepts.why: Many operations want grayscale, other libraries want RGB, and finding objects by colour works far better in HSV.
concepts.body:
A **colour space** is a way of describing a colour with numbers. BGR is one: how much blue, green and red light to mix. Others describe the same colours differently, and some jobs are much easier in one than another. `cv2.cvtColor(img, code)` converts an image between them; the codes read like `COLOR_<from>2<to>`:

- `cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY`: one brightness channel, a weighted sum 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B (green counts most because our eyes are most sensitive to it)
- `cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB`: needed before handing images to other libraries such as matplotlib or Pillow (another Python image library), and to most image-recognition models, which expect RGB
- `cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV`: hue, saturation, value (explained below)
- `cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB`: lightness plus two colour axes, arranged so that equal number differences look like roughly equal colour differences to people; good for measuring how different two colours are and for contrast tweaks

**HSV** separates *which colour* (hue) from *how strong* it is (saturation) and *how bright* (value). A red ball in shade and in sunlight has very different BGR numbers but a similar hue, which is why selecting by colour is done in HSV.

For 8-bit images OpenCV squeezes hue into **0 to 179** (degrees around the circle of colours, divided by 2) so it fits in a byte; S and V use 0 to 255. Red sits at both ends of the hue circle, around 0 and around 179, so selecting red needs two ranges.

Gray to BGR (`COLOR_GRAY2BGR`) does not invent colour; it copies the one channel three times so you can draw coloured shapes and labels on it.

Flipping the channel order with slicing, `img[..., ::-1]`, also turns BGR into RGB, but the result is a view whose values are not stored in plain order in memory, and some cv2 functions reject that. `cvtColor` always returns a fresh, normally laid-out array.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.zeros((1, 3, 3), np.uint8)
img[0] = [(0, 0, 255), (0, 255, 0), (255, 0, 0)]   # red, green, blue (BGR)

gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
print(gray)                 # [[ 76 150  29]]

rgb = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
print(rgb[0, 0])            # [255   0   0]  red is first now

hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
print(hsv[0, :, 0])         # [  0  60 120]  hue in 0..179 (degrees / 2)
print(hsv[0, :, 1:])        # saturation and value are 255
takeaways: `cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_X2Y)` converts between colour spaces
Convert BGR to RGB before passing images to other libraries
HSV separates colour from brightness; 8-bit hue runs 0 to 179
Red wraps around hue 0/179, so it needs two ranges
pitfalls: Using hue thresholds in degrees (0 to 360) on 8-bit HSV images, where hue is halved.

quiz.q: In an 8-bit HSV image from OpenCV, a pure green pixel has hue value...
quiz.explain: Green is 120 degrees, and OpenCV stores hue divided by 2 for uint8 images.

quiz.q: Why is colour segmentation usually done in HSV rather than BGR?
options: Hue stays fairly stable when lighting changes, while BGR values all shift
quiz.explain: HSV puts brightness in its own channel, so a hue range tolerates shadows and highlights.

concepts.name: Drawing shapes and text
concepts.summary: Annotate images in place with cv2.line, rectangle, circle, polylines and putText.
concepts.why: Drawing boxes and labels on an image is how you check, by eye, that your image code found the right things.
concepts.body:
OpenCV's drawing functions **change the image in place**: they write the shape's pixels straight into the array you pass, rather than returning a new image. They take coordinates as `(x, y)` tuples of whole numbers:

- `cv2.line(img, pt1, pt2, color, thickness)`
- `cv2.rectangle(img, top_left, bottom_right, color, thickness)`
- `cv2.circle(img, center, radius, color, thickness)`
- `cv2.polylines(img, [pts], isClosed, color, thickness)` where `pts` is an int32 array of shape `(n, 1, 2)` or `(n, 2)`
- `cv2.putText(img, text, origin, font, scale, color, thickness, lineType)`; the origin is the **bottom-left** corner of the text

Colours are BGR tuples: `(0, 0, 255)` is red. A `thickness` of `-1` (or `cv2.FILLED`) fills the shape. Pass `lineType=cv2.LINE_AA` for **anti-aliased** lines: pixels along the edge get in-between shades, so lines look smooth instead of jagged.

Coordinates must be integers. Positions calculated by other code often come out as floats, so convert them with `int(...)` or `np.round(...).astype(int)` before drawing; recent versions raise an error on floats.

Because drawing changes the array, draw on `img.copy()` when you still need the clean image, for example to keep processing it afterwards.

`cv2.getTextSize(text, font, scale, thickness)` returns the text's width and height plus the baseline (how far letters like g and p hang below), which lets you draw a filled box behind a label so it stays readable on any image. Only a few simple built-in fonts (the Hershey fonts) are available, and they cover only basic Latin letters; for other alphabets or emoji, draw the text with the Pillow library instead.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

canvas = np.zeros((200, 300, 3), np.uint8)
cv2.rectangle(canvas, (20, 30), (140, 120), (0, 255, 0), 2)    # green box
cv2.circle(canvas, (220, 75), 40, (0, 0, 255), -1)             # filled red
cv2.line(canvas, (0, 199), (299, 150), (255, 255, 255), 1, cv2.LINE_AA)

pts = np.array([[160, 180], [200, 140], [240, 180]], np.int32)
cv2.polylines(canvas, [pts], True, (255, 0, 0), 2)              # blue triangle

label = "cat 0.93"
font = cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX
(tw, th), base = cv2.getTextSize(label, font, 0.5, 1)
cv2.rectangle(canvas, (20, 30 - th - base), (20 + tw, 30), (0, 255, 0), -1)
cv2.putText(canvas, label, (20, 30 - base), font, 0.5, (0, 0, 0), 1, cv2.LINE_AA)

print(canvas[75, 220])      # [  0   0 255]  inside the red circle
print(canvas[30, 80])       # [  0 255   0]  on the box edge
takeaways: Drawing functions modify the image in place; copy first if needed
Points are integer (x, y) tuples, colours are BGR
thickness=-1 fills; LINE_AA smooths edges
putText's origin is the text's bottom-left corner
pitfalls: Passing float coordinates from a detector straight into cv2.rectangle.

quiz.q: What does `cv2.circle(img, (50, 20), 10, (255, 0, 0), -1)` draw?
options: A filled blue circle centred at x=50, y=20
An outlined red circle centred at row 50, column 20
A filled red circle centred at x=50, y=20
Nothing, because -1 is an invalid thickness
quiz.explain: Points are (x, y), (255, 0, 0) is blue in BGR, and thickness -1 fills the shape.

concepts.name: Resize, crop, flip and rotate
concepts.summary: Crop with slicing, scale with cv2.resize and the right interpolation, and flip or rotate by 90 degrees.
concepts.why: Many tools, image-recognition models among them, need images at a fixed size and orientation, and the wrong resizing method costs quality.
concepts.body:
**Cropping** needs no cv2 call: slice the array, `img[y1:y2, x1:x2]`. The result is a view, so drawing on it changes the original; add `.copy()` for an independent crop.

`cv2.resize(img, dsize, fx=..., fy=..., interpolation=...)` scales an image. Either pass an explicit size as **`(width, height)`**, or pass `dsize=None` with scale factors `fx`, `fy`. To keep the **aspect ratio** (width divided by height, so the picture isn't stretched), compute one side from the other.

Resizing creates pixels that didn't exist before, so their values must be estimated from the old ones. That estimating is called **interpolation**, and the method matters:

- `cv2.INTER_AREA`: best for shrinking; averages pixels and avoids wavy stripe patterns
- `cv2.INTER_LINEAR` (default): fast and fine for moderate enlarging
- `cv2.INTER_CUBIC` or `INTER_LANCZOS4`: sharper enlargements, slower
- `cv2.INTER_NEAREST`: no blending, each new pixel copies the nearest old one; use it for label images, where each pixel holds a category number (1 = road, 2 = car) and averaging would invent categories that don't exist

`cv2.flip(img, code)` mirrors: `1` left-right, `0` upside down, `-1` both. Left-right flips are also a cheap way to double a collection of example photos.

`cv2.rotate(img, cv2.ROTATE_90_CLOCKWISE)` (also `ROTATE_180`, `ROTATE_90_COUNTERCLOCKWISE`) rotates by right angles exactly, swapping width and height for 90-degree turns. Other angles need a warp, covered in a later lesson.

Many models also expect **letterboxing**: shrink the image to fit inside the target size while keeping its aspect ratio, then fill the leftover strips with a plain colour using `cv2.copyMakeBorder`, like the black bars around a widescreen film.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 256, (480, 640, 3), dtype=np.uint8)

crop = img[100:300, 200:500]                 # rows y, then cols x
print(crop.shape)                            # (200, 300, 3)

small = cv2.resize(img, (320, 240), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)  # (w, h)!
print(small.shape)                           # (240, 320, 3)

half = cv2.resize(img, None, fx=0.5, fy=0.5)
print(half.shape)                            # (240, 320, 3)

target_w = 200                               # keep aspect ratio
h, w = img.shape[:2]
fit = cv2.resize(img, (target_w, round(h * target_w / w)), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
print(fit.shape)                             # (150, 200, 3)

mirrored = cv2.flip(img, 1)
print((mirrored[:, 0] == img[:, -1]).all())  # True
print(cv2.rotate(img, cv2.ROTATE_90_CLOCKWISE).shape)   # (640, 480, 3)
takeaways: Crop by slicing `img[y1:y2, x1:x2]` (a view)
`cv2.resize` takes `(width, height)` or scale factors
INTER_AREA to shrink, LINEAR/CUBIC to enlarge, NEAREST for label images
`cv2.flip` and `cv2.rotate` handle mirrors and right-angle turns
pitfalls: Resizing a label image with the default linear interpolation, which blends neighbouring labels into meaningless values.

quiz.q: `cv2.resize(img, (100, 50))` on a (200, 400, 3) image returns which shape?
quiz.explain: dsize is (width, height), and the array shape is (height, width, channels).

quiz.q: Which interpolation should you use to resize a label image, where each pixel holds a whole-number category?
quiz.explain: Nearest neighbour copies existing labels instead of averaging them into values that mean nothing.

concepts.name: Thresholding and Otsu
concepts.summary: Turn grayscale images into black-and-white masks with fixed, Otsu and adaptive thresholds.
concepts.why: Black-and-white masks are the starting point for finding and measuring objects, and the threshold choice decides their quality.
concepts.body:
**Thresholding** answers a yes/no question for every pixel: is it brighter than a chosen value, the threshold? The answer is a **binary mask**: an image of the same size where the selected pixels are 255 (white) and the rest 0 (black), the image version of the boolean masks you know from NumPy. `cv2.threshold(gray, thresh, maxval, type)` returns a tuple `(used_threshold, result)`:

- `cv2.THRESH_BINARY`: pixels above `thresh` become `maxval`, others 0
- `cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV`: the opposite, handy for dark objects on a light background
- `THRESH_TRUNC`, `THRESH_TOZERO`: cap or zero values instead of making them black-and-white

Picking `thresh` by hand is fragile. A **histogram** counts how many pixels have each brightness; for a bright object on a dark background it shows two bumps, one per group.

Add `cv2.THRESH_OTSU` to the type (and pass 0 as `thresh`) and **Otsu's method** chooses the value that best separates the two bumps. The first return value tells you which threshold it chose.

A single value for the whole image fails when the lighting varies, as with a photographed page that is darker in one corner. `cv2.adaptiveThreshold(gray, 255, method, type, blockSize, C)` computes a separate threshold for each pixel from the `blockSize` x `blockSize` square around it, minus a constant `C`. `ADAPTIVE_THRESH_MEAN_C` uses the plain average of that square, `ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C` a weighted one that counts nearer pixels more. `blockSize` must be odd.

Thresholds expect a **single-channel** image, so convert with `cvtColor` first. Blurring slightly beforehand (`cv2.GaussianBlur`, covered in a later lesson) smooths out random speckles that would otherwise become tiny false spots. To select by colour instead of brightness, use `cv2.inRange` on an HSV image.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
gray = np.full((100, 100), 60, np.uint8)        # dark background
gray[30:70, 30:70] = 190                        # bright square
gray = cv2.add(gray, rng.integers(0, 30, gray.shape, dtype=np.uint8))

t, fixed = cv2.threshold(gray, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
print(t, fixed[50, 50], fixed[5, 5])            # 127.0 255 0

t, otsu = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
print("otsu chose", t)                          # somewhere between the two peaks
print((otsu == 255).sum())                      # 1600  (the 40x40 square)

ramp = np.tile(np.linspace(0, 200, 100, dtype=np.uint8), (100, 1))
ramp[45:55, ::10] += 40                         # faint marks on uneven light
ad = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(ramp, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_MEAN_C,
                           cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 11, -10)
print(ad.dtype, np.unique(ad))                  # uint8 [  0 255]
takeaways: `cv2.threshold` returns (threshold, mask)
Add THRESH_OTSU to let OpenCV pick the threshold
Use adaptiveThreshold when lighting varies across the image
Threshold a single-channel image, ideally lightly blurred
pitfalls: Forgetting that cv2.threshold returns a tuple and treating the whole tuple as the image.

quiz.q: What is the first value returned by `cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)`?
quiz.explain: With THRESH_OTSU the passed threshold is ignored and the computed one is returned.

quiz.q: A scanned page is bright on the left and shadowed on the right. Which approach binarises the text best?
options: adaptiveThreshold with a local block size
quiz.explain: A local, per-neighbourhood threshold adapts to the changing illumination.

concepts.name: Blurring and convolution filters
concepts.summary: Smooth noise with box, Gaussian, median and bilateral filters, and apply your own kernels with filter2D.
concepts.why: Denoising is the first step before thresholding, edges or features, and each filter trades detail for noise differently.
concepts.body:
Real photos contain **noise**: random speckles of wrong brightness, mostly from the camera sensor. A **filter** replaces each pixel with a value computed from its neighbourhood, the small square of pixels around it.

Linear filters compute a weighted sum: multiply each neighbour by a weight and add the results. The small grid of weights is the **kernel**; a 3x3 kernel with every weight 1/9 gives the plain average of the 9 pixels.

- `cv2.blur(img, (5, 5))`: box filter, the plain average
- `cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (5, 5), sigmaX)`: weights fall off with distance along a bell-shaped curve (a Gaussian); the go-to smoother. Kernel sizes must be odd so there is a centre pixel; pass `(0, 0)` with a sigma (how wide the bell is) to let OpenCV pick the size.
- `cv2.medianBlur(img, 5)`: takes the middle value of the sorted neighbours, which removes **salt-and-pepper noise** (scattered pure white and black pixels) completely while keeping edges sharper than averaging. Not linear.
- `cv2.bilateralFilter(img, d, sigmaColor, sigmaSpace)`: averages only pixels that are close *and* similar in colour, so it smooths flat areas but keeps edges. Much slower.

`cv2.filter2D(img, ddepth, kernel)` applies any kernel you define, for example to sharpen or emboss. `ddepth=-1` keeps the input dtype; use `cv2.CV_32F` (float32) when results can go negative or above 255. Sliding a kernel over an image like this is often called **convolution**; strictly, textbook convolution flips the kernel first and filter2D doesn't, which only matters for kernels that aren't symmetric.

At the borders the kernel hangs over the edge of the image. The `borderType` argument decides how the missing pixels are made up; the default `BORDER_REFLECT_101` mirrors the image without repeating the edge pixel.

Kernels like the Gaussian can be split into a pass along rows followed by a pass down columns (they are *separable*), so even large blurs are cheap.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.full((50, 50), 128, np.uint8)
noisy = img.copy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ys, xs = rng.integers(0, 50, (2, 100))
noisy[ys, xs] = 255                              # salt noise

box = cv2.blur(noisy, (5, 5))
gauss = cv2.GaussianBlur(noisy, (5, 5), 0)
median = cv2.medianBlur(noisy, 5)
print(box.max(), gauss.max())                   # still above 128: spikes smeared
print(median.max())                             # 128 -- median removed them

sharpen = np.array([[0, -1, 0], [-1, 5, -1], [0, -1, 0]], np.float32)
step = np.zeros((5, 5), np.uint8); step[:, 2:] = 100
print(cv2.filter2D(step, -1, sharpen)[2])       # [  0   0 200 100 100] clipped
print(cv2.filter2D(step, cv2.CV_32F, sharpen)[2])  # [   0. -100.  200.  100.  100.]
takeaways: Gaussian blur is the default smoother; kernel sizes are odd
Median blur removes salt-and-pepper noise and keeps edges
Bilateral filter preserves edges at a high cost in speed
filter2D applies custom kernels; use a float ddepth for signed results
pitfalls: Using filter2D with ddepth=-1 on uint8 when the result can be negative, silently clipping it to 0.

quiz.q: An image has scattered pure white and black pixels. Which filter removes them best?
quiz.explain: The median ignores outliers in the neighbourhood, so isolated spikes disappear.

concepts.name: Morphological operations
concepts.summary: Clean binary masks with erode, dilate, opening and closing using structuring elements.
concepts.why: Real thresholded masks are full of specks and holes; morphology fixes them before you count or measure objects.
concepts.body:
**Morphology** treats a binary mask as a set of white shapes and grows or shrinks them. It slides a **structuring element** over the mask: a small shape, such as a 3x3 square, created with `cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT | MORPH_ELLIPSE | MORPH_CROSS, (w, h))`. OpenCV's functions call it the kernel.

- `cv2.erode` (**erosion**): a pixel stays white only if the whole structuring element fits inside the white region. Shapes shrink, thin bridges break, small specks vanish.
- `cv2.dilate` (**dilation**): a pixel becomes white if the structuring element touches any white. Shapes grow, small holes and gaps fill.

Combinations via `cv2.morphologyEx(mask, op, kernel)`:

- `MORPH_OPEN` (erode then dilate): removes small white specks while mostly keeping object size
- `MORPH_CLOSE` (dilate then erode): fills small black holes and joins nearby pieces
- `MORPH_GRADIENT`: dilation minus erosion, an outline of each shape
- `MORPH_TOPHAT` and `MORPH_BLACKHAT`: pick out small bright or dark details that stand out from their surroundings

The structuring element's size sets the scale of what gets removed: an opening with a 5x5 square deletes anything thinner than about 5 pixels. `iterations=` repeats the operation.

The conventions assume **white objects on a black background**. If your objects are dark, invert the mask first (or use `THRESH_BINARY_INV`), otherwise erode and dilate swap meanings.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((40, 40), np.uint8)
mask[10:30, 10:30] = 255          # the object
mask[15, 15] = 0                  # a hole inside it
mask[2, 35] = 255                 # a stray speck

k = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT, (3, 3))
opened = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, k)
print(opened[2, 35])              # 0    speck removed
closed = cv2.morphologyEx(opened, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, k)
print(closed[15, 15])             # 255  hole filled

print((mask == 255).sum())                     # 400
print((cv2.erode(mask, k) == 255).sum())       # fewer: shapes shrank
print((cv2.dilate(mask, k) == 255).sum())      # more: shapes grew
edge = cv2.morphologyEx(closed, cv2.MORPH_GRADIENT, k)
print(edge[20, 10], edge[20, 20])              # 255 0  outline only
takeaways: Erode shrinks white regions, dilate grows them
Opening removes small specks, closing fills small holes
The structuring element's size sets the scale of what gets removed
Morphology assumes white objects on black
pitfalls: Applying morphology to dark-on-light masks without inverting, which reverses the effect.

quiz.q: After thresholding, a mask has many isolated white dots around the real objects. Which operation removes them?
quiz.explain: Opening erodes away small white specks and then dilates the survivors back to size.

quiz.q: What does closing (`MORPH_CLOSE`) do first?
quiz.explain: Closing is dilation followed by erosion, which fills holes and gaps.

concepts.name: Gradients and Canny edges
concepts.summary: Measure how brightness changes with Sobel gradients and find clean, thin edges with the Canny detector.
concepts.why: Edges outline objects and are the starting point for finding outlines, detecting lines and many classic measurements.
concepts.body:
An **edge** is where brightness changes sharply, such as the border between a dark object and a light wall. The **gradient** measures that change: how fast brightness rises or falls from one pixel to the next. `cv2.Sobel(gray, ddepth, dx, dy, ksize)` estimates it along x (`dx=1`) or y (`dy=1`).

Use a signed output type such as `cv2.CV_16S` or `cv2.CV_64F`: with `uint8` output, falling brightness (light-to-dark edges) gives negative values that are clipped to zero and lost. Convert back for display with `cv2.convertScaleAbs`, which takes absolute values and turns them into `uint8`.

`cv2.Laplacian` measures how fast the change itself changes; it reacts strongly to fine detail. That makes the **variance** of its result (how spread out the values are) a quick focus measure: blurry images give a low variance.

The **Canny** detector, `cv2.Canny(gray, low, high)`, turns gradients into thin, connected edge lines:

- it smooths the image and computes how strong each gradient is and which way it points,
- it keeps only the strongest pixel across the width of each edge (**non-maximum suppression**), giving lines one pixel wide,
- it applies **hysteresis**: pixels above `high` are edges, and pixels between `low` and `high` survive only if they connect to such a strong edge.

A ratio of about 1:2 or 1:3 between `low` and `high` is typical; a common rule of thumb derives both from the median brightness of the image. Blur first if the image is noisy, or Canny will report texture as edges.

Canny returns a binary `uint8` image (0 or 255), ready for `findContours` or for `cv2.HoughLinesP`, which detects straight line segments.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.zeros((60, 60), np.uint8)
img[:, 30:] = 200                         # vertical step edge at x = 30

gx8 = cv2.Sobel(img[:, ::-1].copy(), cv2.CV_8U, 1, 0)   # dark-to-light reversed
print(gx8.max())                          # 0  -- negative slope clipped away!
gx = cv2.Sobel(img[:, ::-1].copy(), cv2.CV_16S, 1, 0)
print(gx.min())                           # -800  kept with a signed depth
print(cv2.convertScaleAbs(gx).max())      # 255 for display

edges = cv2.Canny(img, 50, 150)
print(np.unique(edges))                   # [  0 255]
print(np.nonzero(edges[30])[0])           # one-pixel wide edge near x = 30

sharp_var = cv2.Laplacian(img, cv2.CV_64F).var()
blurry_var = cv2.Laplacian(cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (9, 9), 0), cv2.CV_64F).var()
print(sharp_var > blurry_var)             # True: a simple blur detector
takeaways: Use a signed ddepth (CV_16S, CV_64F) for Sobel so negative gradients survive
Canny gives thin binary edges using two hysteresis thresholds
Blur noisy images before edge detection
Variance of the Laplacian is a quick sharpness score
pitfalls: Running Sobel with a uint8 output and losing every light-to-dark edge.

quiz.q: In `cv2.Canny(img, 50, 150)`, a pixel with gradient 100 becomes an edge when...
options: Only if it is connected to a pixel above 150
Only if its neighbours are all below 50
quiz.explain: Hysteresis keeps weak (between thresholds) pixels only when they connect to strong edges.

concepts.name: Histograms and contrast
concepts.summary: Measure how brightness is spread across an image with calcHist and improve contrast with equalizeHist and CLAHE.
concepts.why: Histograms reveal badly exposed images and guide threshold choices; CLAHE is a standard fix for flat, low-contrast images.
concepts.body:
A **histogram** counts how many pixels have each brightness. `cv2.calcHist([img], [channel], mask, [bins], [range])` takes lists because it can combine several images and channels; for a gray image use `cv2.calcHist([gray], [0], None, [256], [0, 256])`, which returns float32 counts of shape `(256, 1)` in OpenCV 4 (flat `(256,)` in OpenCV 5). The upper bound of the range is not included, so 256 covers 0 to 255. `np.bincount(gray.ravel(), minlength=256)` gives the same counts.

Histograms tell you a lot at a glance: everything bunched at the left means the photo is too dark, two clear bumps mean a threshold (or Otsu) will work well. A 2-D histogram of hue and saturation describes an object's colours, and two such histograms can be compared with `cv2.compareHist` to find similar-coloured objects.

**Histogram equalisation**, `cv2.equalizeHist(gray)`, remaps brightness values so they are spread evenly over the whole 0 to 255 range, stretching a narrow range of greys. It treats the whole image at once, so it can exaggerate noise and wash out some regions.

**CLAHE** (Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalisation) equalises small tiles of the image separately, and caps how far each tile's contrast may be stretched to limit the noise boost:

```python
clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
out = clahe.apply(gray)
```

For colour images, never equalise B, G and R separately (that shifts the colours). Convert to LAB, apply CLAHE to the L (lightness) channel only, and convert back.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dull = rng.integers(100, 140, (64, 64), dtype=np.uint8)   # low contrast

hist = cv2.calcHist([dull], [0], None, [256], [0, 256])
print(hist.shape, int(hist[:100].sum()))      # (256, 1) 0  -- (256,) in OpenCV 5
print(dull.min(), dull.max())                 # 100 139

eq = cv2.equalizeHist(dull)
print(eq.min(), eq.max())                     # spread to roughly 0..255

clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(4, 4))
print(clahe.apply(dull).std() > dull.std())   # True: more contrast

bgr = cv2.merge([dull, dull, rng.integers(0, 255, (64, 64), dtype=np.uint8)])
lab = cv2.cvtColor(bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB)
l, a, b = cv2.split(lab)
lab = cv2.merge([clahe.apply(l), a, b])       # only lightness changed
out = cv2.cvtColor(lab, cv2.COLOR_LAB2BGR)
print(out.shape)                              # (64, 64, 3)
takeaways: `calcHist` takes lists: images, channels, bins, ranges
equalizeHist spreads intensities globally
CLAHE equalises tiles with a clip limit and amplifies less noise
For colour, equalise the L channel of LAB, not B, G, R
pitfalls: Equalising each BGR channel independently, which distorts the colours.

quiz.q: Why is CLAHE usually preferred to equalizeHist on photos with mixed lighting?
options: It works locally on tiles and clips the histogram, limiting noise amplification
It works on colour images directly without conversion
quiz.explain: Local, contrast-limited equalisation boosts detail in each region without blowing up noise.

concepts.name: Colour masks and bitwise operations
concepts.summary: Select colour ranges with cv2.inRange and combine or apply masks with bitwise_and, or, not.
concepts.why: Picking objects by colour and combining images (green screens, overlays, cut-outs of the region you care about) are built from masks.
concepts.body:
`cv2.inRange(img, lower, upper)` returns a `uint8` mask that is 255 where **every** channel lies within the bounds (both ends included) and 0 elsewhere. On an HSV image this is the classic colour detector:

```python
mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, (35, 80, 60), (85, 255, 255))   # greens
```

For red, whose hue wraps around 0, combine two ranges with `cv2.bitwise_or`.

The bitwise functions combine pixel values bit by bit (the binary digits each number is stored as): `cv2.bitwise_and`, `bitwise_or`, `bitwise_xor`, `bitwise_not`. On 0/255 masks that is simply AND, OR and NOT of the white areas. Their most useful form takes a `mask=` argument: `cv2.bitwise_and(img, img, mask=mask)` keeps the image where the mask is non-zero and blacks out the rest.

To **composite** one image onto another (paste a cut-out object onto a new background), cut a hole in the background with the inverted mask, keep the foreground with the mask, and add the two. `cv2.addWeighted(a, alpha, b, beta, gamma)` blends instead, for semi-transparent overlays such as colour-coded heatmaps.

Masks must be single-channel `uint8` with the same height and width as the image. A NumPy boolean mask works for indexing (`img[mask > 0] = (0, 0, 255)`), but cv2 functions want the `uint8` form. Convert with `mask.astype(np.uint8) * 255`.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.zeros((50, 100, 3), np.uint8)
img[:, :50] = (0, 200, 0)          # green half
img[:, 50:] = (0, 0, 200)          # red half
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)

green = cv2.inRange(hsv, (35, 80, 60), (85, 255, 255))
print(green.dtype, green[0, 10], green[0, 90])   # uint8 255 0

red = cv2.bitwise_or(cv2.inRange(hsv, (0, 80, 60), (10, 255, 255)),
                     cv2.inRange(hsv, (170, 80, 60), (179, 255, 255)))
print(red[0, 90])                                # 255

only_green = cv2.bitwise_and(img, img, mask=green)
print(only_green[0, 90])                         # [0 0 0]  blacked out

bg = np.full_like(img, 255)                      # white background
comp = cv2.add(cv2.bitwise_and(bg, bg, mask=cv2.bitwise_not(green)), only_green)
print(comp[0, 10], comp[0, 90])                  # [  0 200   0] [255 255 255]

overlay = cv2.addWeighted(img, 0.7, bg, 0.3, 0)
print(overlay[0, 10])                            # [ 76 216  76]
takeaways: `cv2.inRange` makes a 0/255 mask from per-channel bounds
Combine masks with bitwise_or/and/not
`bitwise_and(img, img, mask=m)` keeps only the masked region
`addWeighted` blends two images for overlays
pitfalls: Passing a boolean or 3-channel mask to a cv2 function that expects single-channel uint8.

quiz.q: What does `cv2.bitwise_and(img, img, mask=m)` return?
options: img with m blended on top at 50%
The pixels of img where m is non-zero, black elsewhere
The pixels where m is zero
quiz.explain: AND-ing the image with itself is a no-op, and the mask restricts the output to its non-zero pixels.

concepts.name: Contours and shape measurement
concepts.summary: Find object outlines in binary masks and measure their area, bounding boxes, centroids and shape.
concepts.why: Contours turn a mask into countable objects with positions and sizes, the core of classic detection and inspection.
concepts.body:
A **contour** is the outline of one white region in a binary mask, stored as the list of points along its edge. `cv2.findContours(mask, mode, method)` traces them all and returns `(contours, hierarchy)` in OpenCV 4 and later. Each contour is an int32 array of points with shape `(n, 1, 2)`.

- `mode`: `cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL` returns only outer outlines (usually what you want); `RETR_TREE` also returns the outlines of holes, with parent/child links in `hierarchy`.
- `method`: `cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE` keeps only the end points of straight runs, saving memory; `CHAIN_APPROX_NONE` keeps every pixel.

With contours you can measure:

- `cv2.contourArea(c)` and the perimeter, `cv2.arcLength(c, closed=True)`
- `cv2.boundingRect(c)` gives an upright box `(x, y, w, h)`; `cv2.minAreaRect(c)` the tightest rotated box
- `cv2.moments(c)`: sums over the shape (image moments) from which the area and the **centroid**, the shape's centre point at `(m10/m00, m01/m00)`, follow
- `cv2.approxPolyDP(c, eps, True)` simplifies the outline to a polygon; 4 corners suggests a rectangle
- `cv2.convexHull` gives the outline with every dent filled in, like a rubber band stretched around it; circularity `4*pi*area/perimeter**2` is 1 for a perfect circle

Filter by area to drop noise, and sort by area to find the largest object. `cv2.drawContours(img, contours, -1, color, thickness)` draws them; index `-1` means all.

Feed it a clean binary mask (threshold, Canny, morphology first). Old OpenCV 3 returned three values, which is why older tutorials unpack `_, contours, _`.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((100, 160), np.uint8)
cv2.rectangle(mask, (10, 10), (60, 40), 255, -1)
cv2.circle(mask, (110, 60), 25, 255, -1)
mask[90, 5] = 255                               # one-pixel noise

contours, hierarchy = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL,
                                       cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
print(len(contours))                            # 3
objs = [c for c in contours if cv2.contourArea(c) > 20]
for c in sorted(objs, key=cv2.contourArea, reverse=True):
    area = cv2.contourArea(c)
    x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(c)
    m = cv2.moments(c)
    cx, cy = m["m10"] / m["m00"], m["m01"] / m["m00"]
    peri = cv2.arcLength(c, True)
    corners = len(cv2.approxPolyDP(c, 0.02 * peri, True))
    circ = 4 * np.pi * area / peri ** 2
    print(int(area), (x, y, w, h), (round(cx), round(cy)), corners, round(circ, 2))
# 1890 (85, 35, 51, 51) (110, 60) 8 0.87   circle: many corners, round
# 1500 (10, 10, 51, 31) (35, 25) 4 0.74    rectangle: 4 corners
takeaways: findContours needs a binary mask and returns (contours, hierarchy)
RETR_EXTERNAL for outer outlines, RETR_TREE for nested holes
Measure with contourArea, boundingRect, moments, approxPolyDP
Filter tiny contours by area to ignore noise
pitfalls: Running findContours on a noisy, un-thresholded grayscale image and getting thousands of tiny contours.

quiz.q: You only want the outlines of separate objects, ignoring holes inside them. Which mode?
quiz.explain: RETR_EXTERNAL returns only the outermost contours.

quiz.q: How do you compute a contour's centroid x from its moments `m`?
quiz.explain: The first-order moment m10 divided by the area m00 gives the mean x.

concepts.name: Video files and cameras
concepts.summary: Read frames from files and webcams with VideoCapture and write processed video with VideoWriter.
concepts.why: A video is just a series of images, and most live camera programs are a loop over the frames VideoCapture reads.
concepts.body:
A video is a sequence of still images called **frames**, shown quickly one after another; how many per second is the **frame rate** (fps), often 25 or 30. `cv2.VideoCapture(source)` opens a video file, a numbered series of image files (like `img_%03d.png`), a camera by number (`0` is the default webcam) or a network camera's live feed given by its **URL** (web address, such as an `rtsp://` or `http://` link). Check `cap.isOpened()`, then loop:

```python
while True:
    ok, frame = cap.read()
    if not ok:
        break
```

`read()` returns `(False, None)` at the end of a file or when a camera disconnects, so always check `ok`. Each frame is a normal BGR array.

`cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)`, `CAP_PROP_FRAME_COUNT`, `CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH` and `HEIGHT` report the frame rate, number of frames and size. `cap.set(...)` asks a camera for a setting such as its resolution, which the camera's **driver** (the software that controls the device) may ignore. Frame counts stored in video files are sometimes only estimates. Call `cap.release()` when done to free the file or camera.

`cv2.VideoWriter(path, fourcc, fps, (width, height))` writes frames. The **codec** is the method used to compress the frames into the file, chosen by a four-character code such as `cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*"mp4v")` for `.mp4` or `*"MJPG"` for `.avi`. Every frame you write must exactly match the declared size and have 3 channels unless you pass `isColor=False`; frames that don't match are **silently dropped**, leaving an empty file. Which codecs work depends on how your copy of OpenCV was built (which video libraries, such as FFmpeg, it includes).

For a live preview, `cv2.imshow` plus `cv2.waitKey(1)` in the loop shows frames about as fast as they arrive and lets you exit on a key press.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

w, h, fps = 160, 120, 10
out = cv2.VideoWriter("demo.avi", cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*"MJPG"), fps, (w, h))
for i in range(30):
    frame = np.zeros((h, w, 3), np.uint8)
    cv2.circle(frame, (5 * i, 60), 10, (0, 255, 255), -1)   # moving dot
    out.write(frame)
out.release()

cap = cv2.VideoCapture("demo.avi")
print(cap.isOpened(), cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS))   # True 10.0
n = 0
while True:
    ok, frame = cap.read()
    if not ok:
        break
    n += 1
cap.release()
print(n, frame is None)                            # 30 True
takeaways: Loop `ok, frame = cap.read()` and stop when ok is False
VideoCapture opens files, URLs and cameras by index
VideoWriter needs a fourcc, fps and the exact (width, height) of every frame
Release captures and writers when done
pitfalls: Writing frames whose size differs from the VideoWriter's declared size, which produces an empty video without any error.

quiz.q: Your VideoWriter output file is tiny and won't play, yet no error was raised. What is the most likely cause?
options: The frames written had a different size from the one passed to VideoWriter
The fps was not an integer
You called cap.read() instead of cap.grab()
BGR frames must be converted to RGB first
quiz.explain: VideoWriter silently ignores frames that don't match the declared size or channel count.

concepts.name: Background subtraction and optical flow
concepts.summary: Detect moving objects with MOG2/KNN background models and track points between frames with Lucas-Kanade flow.
concepts.why: Motion is the cheapest strong clue in video: it powers people counters, security cameras and shake-free video.
concepts.body:
**Background subtraction** learns what the empty scene looks like and flags pixels that differ from it. `cv2.createBackgroundSubtractorMOG2(history, varThreshold, detectShadows)` describes each pixel's usual values with a few bell curves (a mixture of Gaussians) that slowly adapt over time. Call `fg = sub.apply(frame)` on every frame; the result is a mask with 255 for moving foreground and, if shadow detection is on, 127 for shadows.

Threshold that mask at 200 to drop shadows, clean it up with morphology, then find contours to get the moving blobs. `createBackgroundSubtractorKNN` is an alternative. The model needs some frames to learn the scene, and a moving camera breaks its basic assumption entirely.

**Optical flow** estimates how pixels move between two frames.

- Sparse: `cv2.goodFeaturesToTrack` picks distinct corner points, then `cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK(prev_gray, gray, p0, None)` (the Lucas-Kanade method) follows them, returning the new points, a status array (1 = tracked) and errors. Keep only points with status 1 and pick new ones from time to time as points get lost. The 'Pyr' means it also works on shrunken copies of the frames (an image pyramid), so it can follow larger movements.
- Dense: `cv2.calcOpticalFlowFarneback` gives an `(h, w, 2)` array with the movement (dx, dy) of every pixel, useful for motion heatmaps but much slower.

For following one specific object, OpenCV also provides ready-made trackers such as `cv2.TrackerMIL_create`, while modern systems often combine a neural-network object detector with a lightweight tracker.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

sub = cv2.createBackgroundSubtractorMOG2(history=50, detectShadows=False)
bg = np.full((80, 80), 100, np.uint8)
for _ in range(30):
    sub.apply(bg)                               # learn the empty scene
frame = bg.copy()
frame[30:50, 30:50] = 250                       # an object appears
fg = sub.apply(frame)
print(fg[40, 40], fg[5, 5])                     # 255 0

prev = np.zeros((100, 100), np.uint8)
cv2.rectangle(prev, (30, 30), (60, 60), 255, -1)
nxt = np.roll(prev, (2, 3), axis=(0, 1))        # moved 3 px right, 2 px down
p0 = cv2.goodFeaturesToTrack(prev, maxCorners=4, qualityLevel=0.1, minDistance=5)
p1, st, err = cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK(prev, nxt, p0, None)
moves = (p1 - p0)[st.ravel() == 1].reshape(-1, 2)
print(np.round(moves.mean(axis=0)))             # [3. 2.]  (dx, dy)
takeaways: MOG2/KNN subtractors learn a background model; apply() returns a foreground mask
Shadows are marked 127 in MOG2; threshold them away
calcOpticalFlowPyrLK tracks sparse points; keep only status == 1
Farneback gives dense per-pixel flow at higher cost
pitfalls: Using background subtraction with a moving or zooming camera, where everything looks like foreground.

quiz.q: What does the `status` array returned by calcOpticalFlowPyrLK tell you?
options: The speed of each point in pixels per second
Whether each point was successfully tracked into the new frame
The frame index of each point
quiz.explain: A status of 1 means the flow for that point was found; 0 means it was lost.

concepts.name: Affine and perspective warps
concepts.summary: Rotate, scale and shear with warpAffine, and rectify planes such as documents with a perspective homography.
concepts.why: Aligning, straightening and augmenting images all rely on warps, and the matrix conventions are easy to get wrong.
concepts.body:
An **affine transform** combines rotation, scaling, shifting (**translation**) and **shear** (slanting, like pushing the top of a deck of cards sideways). Straight lines stay straight and lines that run side by side stay side by side. It is stored as a 2x3 float matrix. Build one and apply it:

```python
M = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, angle_deg, scale)   # positive = counter-clockwise
out = cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (w, h))
```

`cv2.getAffineTransform(src3, dst3)` builds the matrix from three pairs of matching points. The output size is the canvas: rotating within the original size cuts off the corners, so for a full rotation compute the size of the rotated image's bounding box and add a shift to the matrix.

A **perspective transform** (a **homography**) is a 3x3 matrix that maps any four-sided shape onto any other. It is how you turn a photo of a tilted document or whiteboard into a flat, straight-on view: `cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src4, dst4)` from four corners (float32 arrays), then `cv2.warpPerspective(img, H, (w, h))`.

To transform **points** rather than images, use `cv2.transform(pts, M)` for affine matrices and `cv2.perspectiveTransform(pts, H)` for homographies; points need shape `(n, 1, 2)` and a float dtype.

Warps work backwards: for each output pixel they look up where it comes from in the source, so `flags=` picks the interpolation (`INTER_NEAREST` for masks), and `borderMode`/`borderValue` fill areas the source doesn't cover. `cv2.invertAffineTransform` and `np.linalg.inv(H)` give the reverse mapping.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.zeros((100, 200, 3), np.uint8)
cv2.rectangle(img, (80, 30), (120, 70), (255, 255, 255), -1)

M = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((100, 50), 90, 1.0)   # 90 deg counter-clockwise
print(M.shape)                                    # (2, 3)
rot = cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (200, 100))
print(rot.shape)                                  # (100, 200, 3) same canvas

src = np.float32([[20, 10], [180, 30], [190, 90], [10, 80]])   # tilted quad
dst = np.float32([[0, 0], [300, 0], [300, 200], [0, 200]])     # flat page
H = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src, dst)
page = cv2.warpPerspective(img, H, (300, 200))
print(page.shape)                                 # (200, 300, 3)

pts = src.reshape(-1, 1, 2)
print(cv2.perspectiveTransform(pts, H).reshape(-1, 2).round().astype(int))
# [[  0   0] [300   0] [300 200] [  0 200]]
takeaways: Affine = 2x3 matrix, applied with warpAffine; perspective = 3x3, warpPerspective
getRotationMatrix2D uses degrees, positive is counter-clockwise
Four point pairs give a homography that can flatten a document
Transform points with cv2.transform / perspectiveTransform, shape (n, 1, 2) float
pitfalls: Passing int32 point arrays to getPerspectiveTransform, which requires float32.

quiz.q: How many point correspondences does cv2.getPerspectiveTransform need?
quiz.explain: A homography has 8 unknown numbers, and each point pair pins down 2 of them, so four pairs are needed.

quiz.q: You rotate an image by 30 degrees with warpAffine and the corners are cut off. Why?
options: warpAffine only supports multiples of 90 degrees
The angle must be given in radians
The output size equals the original, so the rotated corners fall outside the canvas
quiz.explain: The dsize argument fixes the canvas; enlarge it and add translation to keep everything.

concepts.name: Keypoints, descriptors and matching
concepts.summary: Detect ORB or SIFT keypoints, match descriptors between images and estimate a homography robustly with RANSAC.
concepts.why: Feature matching lets you stitch panoramas, find a known object and align images, without any machine learning.
concepts.body:
**Keypoints** are distinctive spots, such as corners or blobs, that can be found again in another photo of the same scene. A **descriptor** is a vector of numbers summarising the small patch around a keypoint, so that the same spot can be recognised elsewhere.

- `cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures)`: fast and free; its descriptors are strings of bits, compared with **Hamming distance** (the number of bits that differ)
- `cv2.SIFT_create()`: descriptors of floats, more robust to changes of scale and lighting, compared with ordinary straight-line (L2) distance; part of the main package since 4.4, when its patent expired
- `cv2.AKAZE_create()`: a good middle ground

`kp, des = detector.detectAndCompute(gray, None)` returns both.

Match with `cv2.BFMatcher(norm)`, which compares every descriptor with every other ('brute force'), or FLANN, which finds approximate matches much faster for large sets. Use `NORM_HAMMING` for ORB and `NORM_L2` for SIFT. Raw matches contain many mistakes; filter them with **Lowe's ratio test**: find the two closest candidates with `knnMatch(des1, des2, k=2)` and keep a match only if the best distance is clearly smaller (for example under 0.75 times) than the second best.

Even filtered matches include some wrong ones (outliers), so estimate the geometry robustly. **RANSAC** repeatedly fits a homography to a few randomly chosen matches and keeps the one most other matches agree with. `cv2.findHomography(src_pts, dst_pts, cv2.RANSAC, 5.0)` returns the matrix and a mask marking the **inliers**, the matches that agree. Many inliers mean the object really is there; the matrix lets you draw its outline or warp one image onto the other. `cv2.USAC_MAGSAC` is a newer, often more accurate alternative to RANSAC.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
img1 = np.zeros((240, 320), np.uint8)
for x, y, w, h, v in zip(*rng.integers([0, 0, 5, 5, 60], [300, 220, 30, 30, 255], (60, 5)).T):
    cv2.rectangle(img1, (int(x), int(y)), (int(x + w), int(y + h)), int(v), -1)
M = np.float32([[1, 0, 25], [0, 1, 15]])             # shift by (25, 15)
img2 = cv2.warpAffine(img1, M, (320, 240))

orb = cv2.ORB_create(500)
kp1, des1 = orb.detectAndCompute(img1, None)
kp2, des2 = orb.detectAndCompute(img2, None)
pairs = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_HAMMING).knnMatch(des1, des2, k=2)
good = [m for m, n in (p for p in pairs if len(p) == 2) if m.distance < 0.75 * n.distance]

src = np.float32([kp1[m.queryIdx].pt for m in good]).reshape(-1, 1, 2)
dst = np.float32([kp2[m.trainIdx].pt for m in good]).reshape(-1, 1, 2)
H, inliers = cv2.findHomography(src, dst, cv2.RANSAC, 3.0)
print(len(good), int(inliers.sum()))                 # e.g. 200+ matches, most inliers
print(H[:2, 2].round())                              # about [25. 15.]: the shift
takeaways: detectAndCompute gives keypoints plus descriptors
ORB uses Hamming distance, SIFT uses L2 distance
Lowe's ratio test removes ambiguous matches
findHomography with RANSAC rejects outliers and returns an inlier mask
pitfalls: Matching ORB's binary descriptors with NORM_L2, which gives meaningless distances.

quiz.q: Why use knnMatch with k=2 and a ratio test instead of just the single best match?
options: It doubles the number of matches
A match whose best and second-best distances are similar is ambiguous and likely wrong
It converts binary descriptors to float
quiz.explain: The ratio test keeps only distinctive matches whose nearest neighbour is clearly better than the next.

concepts.name: Camera calibration and undistortion
concepts.summary: Estimate a camera's intrinsic matrix and lens distortion from chessboard photos, then remove the distortion from images.
concepts.why: Measuring in real-world units, working out where objects are in 3-D, or drawing virtual objects into video all need a calibrated camera.
concepts.body:
A camera is described by its **intrinsic matrix** K and its **distortion coefficients**. K holds the focal lengths `fx`, `fy` (how strongly the lens magnifies, in pixels) and the principal point `cx`, `cy` (where the lens's centre line hits the image, usually near the middle). The distortion coefficients describe how the lens bends straight lines: radial ones (k1, k2, k3) for lines bowing outwards or inwards, strongest near the edges of wide-angle shots, and tangential ones (p1, p2) for a lens mounted slightly tilted.

Calibration recipe:

- Print a chessboard and photograph it 10 to 20 times from different angles and distances, covering the whole frame.
- For each image, `cv2.findChessboardCorners(gray, (cols, rows))` finds the inner corners; refine them with `cv2.cornerSubPix`. `(cols, rows)` counts inner corners, not squares.
- Build the matching real-world 3-D points: a flat grid with z = 0, scaled by the real size of one square.
- `ret, K, dist, rvecs, tvecs = cv2.calibrateCamera(objpoints, imgpoints, image_size, None, None)`.

`ret` is the **reprojection error**: using the fitted camera model, OpenCV predicts where each corner should appear and measures how far off the detected corners are, as a root-mean-square (RMS) average in pixels. Under about 0.5 is good; larger values point to blurry shots, a wrong pattern size or too little variety.

Then `cv2.undistort(img, K, dist)` straightens images; for video, compute the pixel mapping once with `cv2.initUndistortRectifyMap` and apply `cv2.remap` to each frame. `cv2.solvePnP(object_pts, image_pts, K, dist)` recovers the **pose** of a known object (its position and orientation relative to the camera), and `cv2.projectPoints` draws 3-D points onto the image.

The intrinsics are only valid for the resolution and zoom/focus you calibrated with. ChArUco boards (a chessboard combined with printed square markers, in the `aruco` module) work better when the board is only partly visible.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

pattern, square = (7, 5), 30.0                 # inner corners, mm per square
obj = np.zeros((7 * 5, 3), np.float32)
obj[:, :2] = np.mgrid[0:7, 0:5].T.reshape(-1, 2) * square

K_true = np.array([[800, 0, 320], [0, 800, 240], [0, 0, 1]], np.float64)
objpoints, imgpoints = [], []
for rx, ry in [(0.3, 0.1), (-0.2, 0.3), (0.1, -0.3), (0.4, 0.4), (-0.3, -0.2)]:
    rvec = np.array([rx, ry, 0.05]); tvec = np.array([-90.0, -60.0, 600.0])
    pts, _ = cv2.projectPoints(obj, rvec, tvec, K_true, None)   # simulated corners
    objpoints.append(obj); imgpoints.append(pts.astype(np.float32))

rms, K, dist, rvecs, tvecs = cv2.calibrateCamera(objpoints, imgpoints, (640, 480), None, None)
print(rms < 0.01)                              # True: perfect synthetic data
print(K.round())                               # close to fx=fy=800, cx=320, cy=240
print(dist.shape)                              # (1, 5) k1 k2 p1 p2 k3
takeaways: Intrinsics K and distortion coefficients describe the camera
Calibrate from many varied chessboard views; the pattern size counts inner corners
The RMS reprojection error should be well under a pixel
Undistort with undistort, or precomputed maps plus remap for video
pitfalls: Calibrating at one resolution and using the matrix on frames of another resolution or zoom.

quiz.q: calibrateCamera returns an RMS error of 4.2 pixels. What does that suggest?
options: Something is wrong: bad corner detections, wrong pattern size or too few varied views
The lens has strong distortion, which is normal
The image size must be given as (height, width)
quiz.explain: A good calibration reprojects corners within a fraction of a pixel; several pixels indicates a problem.

concepts.name: Running neural networks with cv2.dnn
concepts.summary: Load ONNX neural networks with cv2.dnn, prepare inputs with blobFromImage and run them with only OpenCV installed.
concepts.why: cv2.dnn lets you ship an app that recognises or finds objects in images with only OpenCV installed, no large machine-learning library.
concepts.body:
A **neural network** is a model that has learned from many example images to recognise things: a classifier says what is in the picture, a detector also says where. The learning, called **training**, is done with a large machine-learning library such as PyTorch or TensorFlow. Running an already trained network on new images is **inference**, and that is what OpenCV's dnn module does; it cannot train.

To move a trained network between libraries, export it to **ONNX**, a common file format for neural networks, and load it with `net = cv2.dnn.readNet("model.onnx")` (or `readNetFromONNX`).

Networks take their input as a 4-D float32 array called a **blob**, in **NCHW** layout: N images (the batch), then channels, height and width. `cv2.dnn.blobFromImage` does the usual preparation in one call:

```python
blob = cv2.dnn.blobFromImage(img, scalefactor=1/255, size=(224, 224),
                             mean=(0, 0, 0), swapRB=True, crop=False)
```

- `scalefactor` multiplies pixel values (after `mean` is subtracted)
- `size` resizes; `crop=True` cuts out the centre instead of stretching
- `swapRB=True` turns OpenCV's BGR into the RGB most networks were trained on

Then `net.setInput(blob)` and `out = net.forward()`. What comes out depends on the network: one score per category for classifiers, boxes and scores for detectors, which you decode yourself. Detectors usually report several overlapping boxes for one object; `cv2.dnn.NMSBoxes` keeps the best-scoring box and drops the others that overlap it heavily (non-maximum suppression). Higher-level helpers such as `cv2.dnn.DetectionModel` do some of this for you.

`net.setPreferableBackend` and `setPreferableTarget` choose what does the computing: the default on the processor, CUDA on NVIDIA graphics cards, OpenVINO on Intel hardware or OpenCL, depending on how OpenCV was built. Preparation must match training exactly: wrong scaling, channel order or mean subtraction silently ruins accuracy. OpenCV 5 reworks the dnn engine to support more ONNX models, but the Python workflow stays the same.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.zeros((300, 400, 3), np.uint8)
img[..., 2] = 255                                  # pure red in BGR

blob = cv2.dnn.blobFromImage(img, scalefactor=1 / 255, size=(224, 224),
                             mean=(0, 0, 0), swapRB=True, crop=False)
print(blob.shape, blob.dtype)                      # (1, 3, 224, 224) float32
print(blob[0, :, 0, 0])                            # [1. 0. 0.]  now RGB, scaled

boxes = [[10, 10, 100, 100], [12, 12, 100, 100], [200, 50, 80, 80]]   # x, y, w, h
scores = [0.9, 0.8, 0.75]
keep = cv2.dnn.NMSBoxes(boxes, scores, score_threshold=0.5, nms_threshold=0.4)
print(sorted(np.array(keep).ravel().tolist()))     # [0, 2]  duplicate box removed

# With a real model file:
# net = cv2.dnn.readNet("resnet18.onnx")
# net.setInput(blob); scores = net.forward()      # e.g. shape (1, 1000)
takeaways: cv2.dnn only runs trained networks; train elsewhere and export to ONNX
blobFromImage makes NCHW float32 input: scale, resize, mean, swapRB
Decode outputs yourself and filter overlapping boxes with NMSBoxes
Input preparation must match the network's training exactly
pitfalls: Forgetting swapRB=True for a model trained on RGB images, quietly lowering accuracy.

quiz.q: What shape does `cv2.dnn.blobFromImage(img, size=(320, 240))` produce for one colour image?
quiz.explain: Blobs are NCHW: batch 1, 3 channels, then height 240 and width 320.

concepts.name: How cv2 maps NumPy arrays to cv::Mat
concepts.summary: Understand how cv2 turns arrays into OpenCV's C++ images, why some views or dtypes fail or get copied, and how outputs are created.
concepts.why: Most mysterious cv2 errors in Python come from the array-to-Mat conversion, not from the algorithm itself.
concepts.body:
OpenCV itself is written in C++. Every `cv2` function you call goes through automatically generated glue code, the **Python bindings**, which converts your arguments to C++ types and calls the real function. Images become **cv::Mat**, OpenCV's C++ image type (or the related `cv::InputArray`).

A Mat is a small description (rows, columns, element type, and the step: how many bytes from one row to the next, like a NumPy stride) plus a **pointer**, a value holding the memory address where the pixels live. So a suitable ndarray is **wrapped without copying**: the Mat simply points at the array's own memory.

What counts as suitable:

- Supported dtypes map to Mat element types: `uint8` is CV_8U, plus `int8`, `uint16`, `int16`, `int32`, `float32`, `float64` (OpenCV 5 adds more, such as `bool`, `uint32`, `int64`). `int64` arrays, NumPy's default integer, are rejected or converted by many functions, which is why points should be `int32` or `float32`.
- The last axis becomes the channels (at most 512, `CV_CN_MAX`) when the array is 3-D.
- Rows may be spaced out in memory (strided), but the values within each row must be contiguous. A view like `img[..., ::-1]` steps backwards through the channels (a negative stride), and functions that **write into an argument** (drawing, `out=`/`dst=` parameters) then raise "Layout of the output array is incompatible with cv::Mat". Fix it with `np.ascontiguousarray`.

**In-place** functions like `cv2.rectangle` change your array because the Mat shares its memory. Functions that return a new image create a fresh ndarray on every call; in a loop over video frames, passing a correctly shaped `dst=` array lets OpenCV reuse it instead of making a new **memory allocation** each time.

**Saturation**: cv2 arithmetic and conversions use `saturate_cast`, clamping at the limits instead of wrapping, and rounding float to int to the nearest whole number instead of cutting off the fraction as NumPy's `astype` does.

Read error messages carefully. The bindings often hold several C++ versions of one function for different argument types (**overloading**) and try each in turn, so "Expected Ptr<cv::UMat> for argument" usually means none matched: the array argument had an unsupported dtype or shape.
concepts.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.zeros((50, 50, 3), np.uint8)
rgb_view = img[..., ::-1]                        # negative channel stride
print(rgb_view.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"])            # False
try:
    cv2.rectangle(rgb_view, (5, 5), (20, 20), (255, 0, 0), -1)
except cv2.error as e:
    print("error:", "Layout" in str(e))         # error: True
fixed = np.ascontiguousarray(rgb_view)
cv2.rectangle(fixed, (5, 5), (20, 20), (255, 0, 0), -1)   # works

pts64 = np.array([[1, 1], [10, 1], [10, 10]])    # int64 by default
pts32 = pts64.astype(np.int32)
cv2.fillPoly(img, [pts32], (0, 255, 0))          # int32 is what cv2 expects

f = np.array([[1.6, -0.4, 300.0]], np.float32)
print(f.astype(np.uint8))                        # NumPy: [[1 0 44]] (truncate, wrap)
print(cv2.convertScaleAbs(f))                    # cv2: [[  2   0 255]] round + saturate
takeaways: Suitable ndarrays are wrapped as cv::Mat without copying
Output/in-place arguments must be contiguous within each row: use np.ascontiguousarray
Prefer int32 or float32 for points; int64 often fails
cv2 conversions round and saturate, NumPy astype truncates and wraps
pitfalls: Drawing on `img[..., ::-1]` or another non-contiguous view and getting a cryptic layout error.

quiz.q: Why can cv2.rectangle fail on `img[:, :, ::-1]` but work on `img.copy()`?
options: The view has the wrong dtype
The view's channels are stored with a negative stride, which cv::Mat cannot represent for output
quiz.explain: Mat requires elements within a row to be laid out contiguously; reversing channels breaks that.

quiz.q: `cv2.convertScaleAbs(np.float32([[300.0]]))` returns...
quiz.explain: OpenCV saturates out-of-range values to 255 instead of wrapping modulo 256.

concepts.name: Performance: threads, UMat and vectorising
concepts.summary: Measure and speed up cv2 code with thread control, the T-API's UMat, and by avoiding per-pixel Python loops.
concepts.why: Live video leaves only milliseconds per frame, so knowing where the time goes in cv2 code is essential.
concepts.body:
Start by measuring. `cv2.getTickCount()` and `cv2.getTickFrequency()` give precise timings, as does `time.perf_counter`.

The biggest win is usually removing **Python loops over pixels**. A loop over a 1920x1080 frame visits two million pixels one by one through the Python interpreter; the matching cv2 or NumPy call runs in optimised C++ that also uses **SIMD** instructions, which process several pixels in a single processor step (AVX on Intel and AMD chips, NEON on ARM). `cv2.useOptimized()` reports whether these optimised code paths are switched on (they are by default).

Many OpenCV functions also split their work across several **threads**: separate lines of execution that run at the same time on different processor cores. They come from OpenCV's own **thread pool**, a set of threads kept ready for reuse. `cv2.setNumThreads(n)` sets how many; `cv2.getNumThreads()` reports it.

If you already split the work at a higher level, for example over several worker **processes** (separate running copies of your program) from Python's `multiprocessing` module, set it to 0 or 1 inside each worker. Otherwise every process starts a full set of threads and they fight over the cores (**oversubscription**), which makes everything slower.

The **Transparent API** (T-API) uses `cv2.UMat` arrays instead of ndarrays. Functions called with UMat inputs may run on a graphics processor (**GPU**) through **OpenCL**, a standard way to run calculations on graphics chips, and return UMats; call `.get()` to copy the result back into an ndarray. It pays off only for chains of heavy operations on large images, because every copy to and from the graphics chip costs time. Check `cv2.ocl.haveOpenCL()`.

Other levers:

- Work at lower resolution when you can: halving width and height cuts most costs by four.
- Reuse output arrays with `dst=` arguments in loops.
- Use a **look-up table** with `cv2.LUT` for per-pixel mappings such as gamma correction (a brightness curve): compute the answer for all 256 possible values once, then just look each pixel up.
- CUDA functions (`cv2.cuda`, for NVIDIA graphics cards) exist only in builds you compile yourself; the packages pip installs don't include them.
concepts.code:
import time
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 256, (720, 1280), dtype=np.uint8)

gamma = 0.5
table = np.array([((i / 255) ** gamma) * 255 for i in range(256)]).astype(np.uint8)

t = time.perf_counter()
